title: The Science of Education
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Prompted by rediscovering John Dewey's 1929 book The Sources of a Science of Education while researching the foreword to his own forthcoming book, Paul Kirschner uses Dewey's century-old argument to critique the modern habit of converting single research findings directly into classroom prescriptions. Dewey's core claim, Kirschner explains, is that genuine science is cumulative and coherent, a connected explanatory system rather than a heap of individually impressive studies, and that no single scientific conclusion can be converted into a fixed rule of educational practice because laboratory findings gain their explanatory power precisely by stripping away the complexity a real classroom restores. Kirschner extends this into a warning against treating cognitive psychology findings as automatically educational just because a paragraph of classroom implications is appended, arguing that understanding a memory mechanism in an experiment and knowing how to use that understanding to teach fractions are genuinely different intellectual problems. He closes by arguing, following Dewey, that classroom practice must inform science just as much as science informs practice, that teachers who are reduced to mere implementers of research 'recipes' will inevitably distort conclusions before they reach students, and that a mature science of education should make practitioners simultaneously more confident in evidence and more resistant to treating any single study as a universal commandment.
points: Kirschner's central Dewey-derived distinction is between scientific findings as 'laws' (fixed rules for action) versus as 'rules for better observation and inquiry,' arguing research should sharpen a teacher's judgment rather than replace it.

He highlights Dewey's pointed claim that treating research as rigid prescription is itself a departure from scientific method, quoting Dewey's line that only the 'third or fourth-rate man' or the 'unskilled day laborer' follows research as an imposed course of action.

His engineering analogy clarifies why psychology findings aren't automatically 'educational science': just as math and mechanics are indispensable sources for bridge-building without being the science of bridge-building itself, cognitive psychology is a source for teaching, not teaching science itself.

Kirschner explicitly rejects the one-way 'laboratory to classroom' pipeline model of research translation, arguing (with Dewey) that educational practice supplies the problems that give research its point and is the arena where scientific conclusions get tested and revised.

He frames teacher professional judgment as 'an almost unworked mine,' warning that reducing teachers to pure implementers of prescribed research findings will distort those findings before they ever reach students, an argument for practitioner voice in educational research.
quotes: The trouble begins when we confuse the use of science in education with the direct application of individual research results to education. Those aren't the same thing.
Scientific knowledge grows as a connected structure, an organism, rather than as a heap of individually impressive studies, a clump of cells.
No genuine science is formed by isolated conclusions, however exact the measurements or impeccable the technique by which those conclusions were reached.

It is not the capable engineer who treats scientific findings as imposing upon him a certain course which is to be rigidly adhered to: it is the third or fourth-rate man who adopts this course. Even more, it is the unskilled day laborer who follows it.

Understanding a memory phenomenon during an experiment and deciding how that understanding should be used when teaching fractions, historical causation, reading, or electrical circuits are different intellectual problems.
Dewey thought classroom teachers should contribute to the development of educational knowledge because they're in direct contact with the phenomena the science is trying so hard to understand.
It's not a conveyor belt running from laboratory to classroom, but a two-way street that travels in both directions with science informing practice and practice informing science.
